title: Top K Frequent Elements
prompt: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the k most frequent elements. You may return the answer in any order. It is guaranteed the answer is unique. Can you design an algorithm that beats the O(n log n) of sorting all elements by frequency?
blurb: Count then select — a size-k min-heap gives O(n log k), and bucket sort by frequency achieves O(n) by indexing counts into an array of buckets.

rubric.label: Problem understanding
rubric.description: Recognizes this is 'count frequencies, then take the k largest by count', notes the answer is unique (no tie-break needed), and that full sort by frequency is O(n log n) — the prompt asks for better.

rubric.label: Approach
rubric.description: Builds a frequency map, then selects top k via a size-k min-heap (O(n log k)) or bucket sort by frequency (O(n)). Can articulate the Quickselect-on-unique-elements alternative for O(n) average.

rubric.label: Correctness
rubric.description: Heap: keeps exactly k by popping the smallest-count when size exceeds k; extracts k elements. Bucket: index = frequency (0..n), place elements in bucket[freq], scan buckets high-to-low collecting until k are gathered. No off-by-one on bucket size (n+1).

rubric.label: Complexity analysis
rubric.description: Heap O(n log k) time / O(n + k) space. Bucket sort O(n) time / O(n) space. Quickselect O(n) average. Explains why bucket sort escapes the log factor: frequency is bounded by n, so it can be used as an array index.

rubric.label: Code quality
rubric.description: Clean Counter/hash-map build, a single heap or a clean bucket array of lists; collection loop terminates correctly at k without over-collecting.

rubric.label: Edge cases
rubric.description: k == number of distinct elements (return all), all elements identical (one bucket), single element, k=1 (the mode), negatives, and the answer-is-unique guarantee removing tie ambiguity.

rubric.label: Testing
rubric.description: Tests k = distinct count and an all-same array; verifies the bucket scan direction (high frequency first) and that exactly k elements are returned.

rubric.label: Communication
rubric.description: Explains the count-then-select decomposition and why frequency being bounded by n unlocks the linear bucket-sort trick.

constraints: 1 <= k <= number of distinct elements in nums
The answer is guaranteed to be unique

examples.explanation: 1 occurs 3 times, 2 occurs twice, 3 once. The two most frequent are 1 and 2.
A single distinct element; it is trivially the most frequent.

test_cases.expected: [1,2,3,4] — k equals the distinct count, return all (any order)
[7] — all identical, a single bucket at frequency 4

reference.optimal_time: O(n) with bucket sort (or Quickselect average); O(n log k) with a size-k heap
reference.optimal_space: O(n) for the frequency map and buckets; O(n + k) for the heap variant

approaches.name: count + full sort by frequency
approaches.idea: Build a frequency map, sort the distinct elements by count descending, take the first k. Simple and correct but sorts all m distinct elements even though only k are needed.

approaches.name: count + size-k min-heap
approaches.idea: Build the frequency map. Push (count, element) into a min-heap; whenever it exceeds size k, pop the smallest count. After processing all distinct elements the heap holds the k most frequent. Beats full sort when k << number of distinct elements, and is the natural streaming choice.

approaches.name: optimal: bucket sort by frequency
approaches.idea: Build the frequency map. Create buckets indexed 0..n where bucket[f] is the list of elements that occur exactly f times (a count can be at most n). Iterate f from n down to 1, appending each bucket's elements to the result until it holds k. Because frequency is bounded by n, it serves directly as an array index, eliminating any comparison sort and giving strict O(n).

approaches.name: Quickselect on distinct elements
approaches.idea: Put the distinct elements in an array and Quickselect by frequency to place the kth-most-frequent at its rank, then take one side. O(n) average like the k-th-largest problem, but with more bookkeeping than bucket sort; worth mentioning as the partition-based alternative.

follow_ups: Top K Frequent WORDS — same idea but ties broken lexicographically, which forces a custom comparator in the heap and a sort within each frequency bucket.
Streaming / online top-k over an unbounded feed — approximate structures (Count-Min Sketch + a heap of heavy hitters, the Space-Saving algorithm) when exact counts don't fit in memory.
k can be as large as the number of distinct elements — when does full sort become just as good as bucket sort in practice?
Return the top k in sorted (descending frequency) order rather than any order — add a final sort of just the k results, O(k log k).
Very large k close to m — compare heap vs bucket vs Quickselect and reason about which wins for that regime.
reference.reference_solution:
Bucket sort (O(n)): topKFrequent(nums, k): count = frequency map of nums. buckets = [[] for _ in range(len(nums)+1)]  // index = frequency, max frequency is n. for val, freq in count.items(): buckets[freq].append(val). res = []. for f in range(len(nums), 0, -1):     // high frequency first. for val in buckets[f]: res.append(val); if len(res) == k: return res. return res. The insight: a frequency can be at most n, so it is a valid array index — no comparison sort needed, hence linear.

Heap alternative (O(n log k)): count = frequency map; heap = []. for val, freq in count.items(): heappush(heap, (freq, val)); if len(heap) > k: heappop(heap)  // drop the least frequent so far. return [val for freq, val in heap]. Prefer the heap when k << distinct count or the data is streamed; prefer bucket sort for the strict O(n) guarantee on a batch.
pitfalls: Bucket array sized n instead of n+1, dropping the element(s) that occur exactly n times.
Scanning buckets low-to-high (least frequent first) and returning the wrong k.
Over-collecting past k when a single bucket holds several elements — stop as soon as k are gathered.
Heap version: using a max-heap of all m elements (O(m log m)) instead of a size-k min-heap, forfeiting the log-k advantage.
Assuming ties need breaking — the base problem guarantees a unique answer, but Top K Frequent Words does not (surface this in the follow-up).

interviewer_notes: The prompt explicitly invites beating O(n log n), so the signal ladder is: count + full sort (weak) -> size-k min-heap O(n log k) (mid) -> bucket sort O(n) (strong). Let them build the frequency map first — everyone does. If they stop at the heap, ask 'can you drop the log factor?' The key realization to listen for is that a count is bounded by n and can therefore index an array — that's what unlocks bucket sort; if they don't see it, nudge with 'what's the largest a frequency can be?'. Stay silent through implementation but watch the bucket sizing (n+1) and scan direction (high-to-low). Good testing tell: do they check k = distinct count and an all-same array? Escalations: Top K Frequent Words (tie-break comparator complexity) and, for senior/staff, the streaming approximate version (Count-Min Sketch / Space-Saving) when exact counting won't fit in memory.
